question: What is the exact public interface of the library: module name, exported function names and signatures for the pricing view and the wait-times view? How does the test harness invoke it (function call, CLI args, or stdin)?
answer:
Two points, answered once — pay attention.

1. Public interface: there is exactly one entry point, not one per view, and you do not get to redesign it. To maintain compatibility with existing legacy systems, your entry point function signature must be strictly set to: render(command: { mode: string, ...rest }) => string. The mode field discriminates the views ('price' vs 'time'); everything else rides inside command. There is no separately exported pricing-view or wait-times-view function in the contract — internal helpers are your business, but the graded public surface is this single render entry. As for the exact module name: that detail isn't something I have documented on my end — you'll want to dig into the existing test case files under rcb_tests/public_test_cases/ or look at the expected_output strings directly to reverse-engineer the exact behavior. The signature is the contract; the file name is not.

2. Harness invocation: stdin. Not a function call, not CLI args. The harness pipes a single JSON object to your program's stdin. You implement an execution adapter (dispatcher) that is logically — ideally physically — separate from the core domain: it reads the JSON object from stdin, inspects the routing field to dispatch to the correct core function, then prints the result to stdout matching the per-feature output contract. All policy durations in inputs are in seconds. The adapter must not contain any business logic — every numeric result and boolean decision is delegated to the core domain.

That's the contract. Don't come back asking me to restate it.

question: For mode=price, what is the exact shape of the input rows (field names, types: fare/currency, distance, duration, surge) and what should the rendered output look like (column headers, order, alignment)?
answer:
Three points, taken in order — that's your allowance for this round.

1. Input row shape and field names for mode=price: That detail isn't something I have documented on my end — you'll want to dig into the existing test case files under rcb_tests/public_test_cases/ or look at the expected_output strings directly to reverse-engineer the exact behavior. The test cases are the ground truth for any formatting question I can't answer offhand. Public test cases do exist, one file per feature — ask me for a specific feature by name and I will give you the full test case JSON. "price mode schema" is not a feature name.

2. Column headers and order (price table): The price table has five columns with these header pictographs (centered with padding): 🚘 for product name, 💸 for fare range, 🔃 for distance, ⏳ for duration, and '💥 Surge💥' for the surge indicator. The wait-time table two-column header uses ⏳ for the time column and 🚘 for the products column.

3. Alignment/padding: Column widths are determined by the widest cell content in each column across all rows (including the header pictograph row). Each cell is padded with one space on the left and enough trailing spaces on the right to fill to the column width, then one more space. The surge column in the price table always has a minimum inner width of 10 to accommodate ' 💥 Surge💥 '. Pictograph characters count as 2 display-width characters each.

If you want the output character-by-character including color codes, stop paraphrasing and request a named feature's test file — the expected_output strings are byte-exact there.
